In [[physics]] and [[mathematics]], the '''Golden–Thompson inequality''' is a [[Trace inequalities|trace inequality]] between [[Matrix_exponential|exponentials]] of symmetric and Hermitian matrices proved independently by {{harvtxt|Golden|1965}} and {{harvtxt|Thompson|1965}}. It has been developed in the context of [[statistical mechanics]], where it has come to have a particular significance.

== Statement ==
The Golden–Thompson inequality states that for (real) symmetric or (complex) [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian matrices]] ''A'' and ''B'', the following [[trace inequality]] holds:

:<math> \operatorname{tr}\, e^{A+B} \le \operatorname{tr} \left(e^A e^B\right).</math>

This inequality is well defined, since the quantities on either side are real numbers. For the expression on the right hand side of the inequality, this can be seen by rewriting it as <math>\operatorname{tr}(e^{A/2}e^B e^{A/2})</math> using the [[Trace (linear algebra)#Cyclic property|cyclic property of the trace]].

Let <math>\|\cdot \|</math> denote the [[Frobenius norm]], then the Golden–Thompson inequality is equivalently stated as<math display="block">\|e^{A+B}\| \leq \|e^A e^B \|.</math>

=== Motivation ===

The Golden–Thompson inequality can be viewed as a generalization of a stronger statement for real numbers. If ''a'' and ''b'' are two real numbers, then the [[Exponential_function|exponential]] of ''a+b'' is the product of the exponential of ''a'' with the exponential of ''b'':
:<math> e^{a+b} = e^a e^b .</math>
If we replace ''a'' and ''b'' with [[commuting matrices]] ''A'' and ''B'', then the same inequality <math> e^{A+B} = e^A e^B</math> holds.

This relationship is '''not''' true if ''A'' and ''B'' do not commute. In fact, {{harvtxt|Petz|1994}} proved that if ''A'' and ''B'' are two Hermitian matrices for which the Golden–Thompson inequality is verified as an equality, then the two matrices commute. The Golden–Thompson inequality shows that, even though <math>e^{A+B}</math> and <math>e^Ae^B</math> are not equal, they are still related by an inequality.

=== Proof ===
{{Math theorem|name=Golden inequality|note={{harvtxt|Golden|1965}}|math_statement=

If <math display="inline">A, B</math> are Hermitian and positive semidefinite, then <math display="block">\operatorname{tr}((AB)^{2^{n}}) \leq \operatorname{tr}((A^{2^1}B^{2^1})^{2^{n-1}}) \leq \operatorname{tr}((A^{2^2}B^{2^2})^{2^{n-2}}) \leq \dots \leq \operatorname{tr}(A^{2^n}B^{2^n})</math>
}}

{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=Proof}}
{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=

If <math display="inline">\operatorname{tr}((AB)^{2^{n}}) \leq \operatorname{tr}((A^{2^1}B^{2^1})^{2^{n-1}})</math> for all <math display="inline">n</math>, then all the other inequalities are also proven as special cases of it. So it suffices to prove that inequality.

<math display="inline">n=0</math> case is trivial.

<math display="inline">n = 1</math> case. Since <math display="inline">A, B</math> are Hermitian and PSD, we can split <math display="inline">A</math> to <math display="inline">(\sqrt A)^2</math>, which allows us to write <math display="inline">\operatorname{tr}(ABAB) = \|\sqrt A B \sqrt A\|^2</math>, meaning it is a non-negative real number.

Now by [[Cauchy–Schwarz inequality]],

<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
              \operatorname{tr}(ABAB) &= \langle AB, BA\rangle \\
              &\leq \|AB\| \|BA\| \\
              &= \|AB\|^2\\
              &= \operatorname{tr}(ABBA)\\
              &= \operatorname{tr}(AABB)
              \end{aligned}</math> 

<math display="inline">n \geq 2</math> case. Define two sequences of matrices <math display="block">
              a_k := (AB)^{2^{n-k}}(BA)^{2^{n-k}}, \quad b_k := (BA)^{2^{n-k}}(AB)^{2^{n-k}}
              </math> which, by construction, are Hermitian and positive semidefinite.

For any <math display="inline">N</math>, by the cyclic property of trace, <math display="block">\begin{cases}\operatorname{tr}(a_k^N) &= \operatorname{tr}((a_{k+1} b_{k+1})^N) =  \operatorname{tr}(b_k^N), \quad \forall k \in 0:n-1 \\\operatorname{tr}(a_n^N) &= \operatorname{tr}((AABB)^N) = \operatorname{tr}(b_n^N)\end{cases}</math>

By the same argument as <math display="inline">n=1</math> case, <math>\operatorname{tr}((AB)^{2^{n}}) \leq \operatorname{tr}(a_1)</math>. Apply Cauchy–Schwarz, and the cyclic equalities, <math display="block">\begin{aligned}
              \operatorname{tr}(a_1) &= \operatorname{tr}(a_2b_2) \\
              &= \langle a_2,b_2\rangle \\
              &\leq \|a_2\| \|b_2\|  \\
              &= \|a_2\|^2\\
              &= \operatorname{tr}(a_2 a_2)
              \end{aligned}</math>

If <math display="inline">n = 2</math>, then <math display="inline">\operatorname{tr}(a_2a_2) = \operatorname{tr}((AABB)^2)</math>.

Otherwise, by induction, <math>
              \operatorname{tr}(a_2 a_2) = \operatorname{tr}((a_3b_3)^2) \leq \operatorname{tr}(a_3a_3b_3b_3)
              </math> and continuing the same argument,<math>
              \operatorname{tr}(a_3a_3b_3b_3) \leq \operatorname{tr}(a_3^4)
              </math>. This continues until we obtain <math display="inline">\leq \operatorname{tr}(a_n^{2^{n-1}}) = \operatorname{tr}((AABB)^{2^{n-1}})</math>.
}}
{{hidden end}}

{{Math theorem|name=Golden–Thompson inequality|note={{harvtxt|Thompson|1965}}|math_statement=

Given Hermitian matrices <math display="inline">A, B</math>,

<math display="block">\operatorname{tr}(e^{A+B}) \leq \operatorname{tr}(e^A e^B)</math> 

}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof= 

By the Lie product formula, <math display="inline">\operatorname{tr}(e^{A+B}) = \lim_n \operatorname{tr}((e^{A/2^n}e^{B/2^n})^{2^n})</math>.

By the Golden inequality, <math display="inline">\operatorname{tr}((e^{A/2^n}e^{B/2^n})^{2^n}) \leq \operatorname{tr}(e^A e^B)</math>.
}}

== Generalizations ==

=== Other norms ===

In general, if ''A'' and ''B'' are Hermitian matrices and <math>\|\cdot\|</math> is a [[unitarily invariant norm]], then {{Harvard citation|Bhatia|1997|loc=Theorem IX.3.7}}
:<math>\|e^{A+B}\| \leq \|e^{A}e^B\| . </math>
The standard Golden–Thompson inequality is a special case of the above inequality, where the norm is the Frobenius norm.

The general case is provable in the same way, since unitarily invariant norms also satisfy the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. {{Harvard citation|Bhatia|1997|loc=Exercise IV.2.7}}

Indeed, for a slightly more general case, essentially the same proof applies. For each <math display="inline">p \geq 1</math>, let <math display="inline">\|A\|_p^p := \operatorname{tr}(AA^*)^{p/2}</math> be the [[Schatten norm]].

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|note=|math_statement= 

For any integer <math display="inline">N \geq 1</math>, <math display="inline">
          \|e^{A+B}\|_{2^N} \leq \|e^{A}e^{B}\|_{2^N} 
          </math>.
For any integer <math display="inline">N \geq 0</math>, 
<math display="inline">\|e^{A+B}\|_{2^N} \leq \|e^{A/2}e^{B}e^{A/2}\|_{2^N}</math>.

At <math display="inline">N \to\infty</math> limit, we obtain the [[operator norm]] <math display="inline">\|e^{A+B}\|_{op} \leq \|e^{A}e^{B}\|_{op} = \|e^{A/2}e^{B}e^{A/2}\|_{op}</math>.
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof {{harvtxt|Tao|2010}}|proof=

It suffices to show that <math display="inline">\operatorname{tr}((e^{A+B})^{2^N}) \leq \operatorname{tr}((e^{2A}e^{2B})^{2^{N-1}})</math>. 
<math display="block">
          \operatorname{tr}((e^{A+B})^{2^N}) = \lim_n \operatorname{tr}((e^{2^{N-n}A}e^{2^{N-n} B})^{2^n}) \leq \lim_n \operatorname{tr}((e^{2A}e^{ 2B})^{2^{N-1}})
          </math> by the Golden inequality.

The second claim is proven similarly.
}}

{{Math theorem|name=Corollary|note=|math_statement= Given Hermitian <math display="inline">A, B</math>, if <math display="inline">e^A \preceq e^B</math> then <math display="inline">A \preceq B</math>.
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof {{harvtxt|Tao|2010}}|proof=

For any <math display="inline">x</math>, we have <math display="inline">\langle e^Ax, x\rangle \leq \langle e^Bx, x\rangle</math>, thus <math display="inline">\|e^{A/2}x\|\leq \|e^{B/2}x\|</math>.

Thus <math display="inline">e^{-B/2}e^{A/2}</math> is a contraction map, thus <math display="inline">\|e^{-B/2}e^{A/2}\|_{op} \leq 1</math>, thus <math display="inline">\|e^{A/2 - B/2}\|_{op} \leq 1</math>, thus all eigenvalues of <math display="inline">(A/2 - B/2)</math> are nonpositive, thus <math display="inline">A \preceq B</math>.
}}

=== Multiple matrices ===
The inequality has been generalized to three matrices by {{harvtxt|Lieb|1973}} and furthermore to any arbitrary number of Hermitian matrices by {{harvtxt|Sutter|Berta|Tomamichel|2016}}. A naive attempt at generalization does not work: the inequality
:<math>\operatorname{tr}(e^{A+B+C}) \leq |\operatorname{tr}(e^Ae^Be^C)|</math>
is false. For three matrices, the correct generalization takes the following form:

:<math> \operatorname{tr}\, e^{A+B+C} \le \operatorname{tr} \left(e^A \mathcal{T}_{e^{-B}} e^C\right),
</math>

where the operator <math>\mathcal{T}_f</math> is the derivative of the [[Logarithm of a matrix|matrix logarithm]] given by <math> \mathcal{T}_f(g) = \int_0^\infty \operatorname{d}t \, (f+t)^{-1} g (f+t)^{-1} </math>. 
Note that, if <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> [[Commuting_matrices|commute]], then <math> \mathcal{T}_f(g) = gf^{-1}</math>, and the inequality for three matrices reduces to the original from Golden and Thompson.

{{harvs|txt|first=Bertram|last=Kostant|year=1973|authorlink=Bertram Kostant}} used the [[Kostant convexity theorem]] to generalize the Golden–Thompson inequality to all compact [[Lie group|Lie groups]].
